chapters.title: Chapter 8: Persistence, Persistence (Dealing with people who refuse to let go)

assets.visual_frame_description: A conference room at a midsize travel agency. Mike Fedder, in shirtsleeves, sits across from Tommy, a preppy young man in a blazer whose folder bulges with proposal material. The wall clock reads forty minutes past the agreed ten-minute meeting, and the player sees a floating tag above Tommy each time Mike declines a step of the proposal.
assets.player_mission: Scrub Tommy's verbal responses for the cue that marks someone who refuses to let go. Identify the single most alarming pattern in how he reacts each time Mike says no, and justify your pick against book evidence.
key_concepts: Refusing to hear no is a clear signal of trouble in any context.
Tommy converted each refusal into a new commitment: no opening meant he would quote start anyway and formalize it when something opened up.
Persistence is treated in American culture as a mark of success, which blinds observers to its danger when it is unwanted.
A request framed as a brief ten-minute meeting expanded into a formal partnership proposal without invitation.
Projecting onto others commitments that were not expressed and are not present is a feature of people who do not let go.
Mike kept predicting Tommy's behavior by applying his own standards for behavior, a faulty method throughout the case.
The language of entitlement, attachment, and rejection must be understood to predict the small behaviors of persistent pursuers.
Contact is fuel for the fire, and Tommy was someone who did not need much fuel.
Victims often ask how a pursuer 'will respond,' when the pursuer does not speak the same language of ordinary logic.
"Maybe" is sometimes perceived as "definitely" by people who do not want to hear the refusal.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the persistence-profile signal that de Becker calls refusing to hear no: each refusal is treated as a negotiable detail rather than a decision. The book claims this is a clear signal of trouble in any context, because the pursuer's persistence is driven by his own alternate perception, not by the accuracy of his hopes.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Verbal responses to rejection during the pitch
assets.question: During the forty-minute meeting, Tommy hears no several times. Which of the following response patterns is the strongest cue that Tommy is a person who refuses to let go?
assets.correct_cue: Tommy never registers a no as a decision; each refusal is instantly restructured into a path forward. When Mike says he does not work with outside agents, Tommy answers, "I can join the team full time." When Mike says there is no opening, Tommy answers, "Oh, I can start anyway, and then we'll formalize it when something opens up." When Mike defers to Marlene's uncertain wedding plans, Tommy later calls Marlene herself to get "a time frame" so he can be "ready to come to work." The book marks this pattern explicitly: "It was refusing to hear 'no,' a clear signal of trouble in any context." The cue is not enthusiasm, effort, or irritation at being kept waiting; it is the systematic conversion of rejection into a new beginning.
distractors: Tommy is irritated that he was kept waiting a few minutes past two o'clock, showing he lacks patience with the arrangement.
Tommy has prepared a thick folder of material, proving his idea is genuinely valuable and worth considering.
Tommy lights up with enthusiasm when he hears about the travel agency's expansion, demonstrating genuine passion for the business.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is entitlement wrapped in the cultural myth that persistence pays. Because Tommy evaluates the interaction from his own alternate perception, a refusal is not information about Mike's wishes; it is an obstacle to work around. De Becker notes this culture teaches that hanging in there against all odds is an attribute of success, so observers like Mike initially read 'persistent, mark of those who succeed' when they should read a refusal-to-hear-no profile.

assets.visual_frame_description: A cluttered kitchen table in the Fedder home. A Federal Express envelope lies open next to a signed-and-waiting letter of reference. Tommy's face hovers in a thought bubble flipping through plausible reactions: gratitude, closure, acceptance. The player must decide what the request really is for.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the reference-letter request for its true function. Decide whether answering it closes the relationship or feeds it, and select the cue that reveals the request's real purpose.
key_concepts: People who refuse to let go often make small requests that appear reasonable, like Tommy's letter of reference.
The real purpose of such requests is to cement attachment or gain new reasons for contact.
Even a polite, noncommittal reply can be used as fresh fuel because contact is fuel for the fire.
Mike left a message declining to sign the letter, and within hours Tommy replied with insults, showing the request was a hook, not a need.
Tommy's angry demand to have the unsigned letter mailed back manufactured a new grievance when the first purpose failed.
Victims become obsessed with making the harassment stop just as the pursuer is obsessed with getting a response.
Guilt is usually the first button a pursuer pushes, then harassment, then insult.
With each contact, the victim buys another six weeks of pursuit.
The pursuer's subtext is always the same: I will not allow you to ignore me.
A reasoned management plan that appears to be doing nothing is a communication to the pursuer every bit as clear as direct contact.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the reasonable-request cue: a small favor that appears legitimate but whose function is to cement attachment or create new reasons for contact. The book shows that replying, even with a refusal, engages the pursuer and buys another six weeks, because any response becomes the issue.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: The function behind a routine favor request
assets.question: Tommy sends a Federal Express envelope asking Mike to sign a letter of reference for his bank. Why does de Becker treat this request as a warning cue rather than a reasonable favor?
assets.correct_cue: The request looks perfectly routine, but the book states outright that people who refuse to let go 'often make small requests that appear reasonable, like Tommy's letter of reference, though the real purpose of such requests is to cement attachment or gain new reasons for contact.' The cue is the timing and function: the request arrives right after Mike declared the relationship finished, and its real product is a call-back, a reply, or a returned letter, not bank paperwork. The evidence is in what followed: Mike's polite answering-machine refusal triggered an insulting tirade ('I'm not surprised you didn't have the courage to talk with me directly') and a new grievance (return the letter), proving the request was an engagement device.
distractors: The request is a genuine professional need because Tommy must show the bank a reference and Mike is the only business owner he knows.
Polite refusal on the answering machine resolves the matter because Tommy finally receives a clear, final answer.
Helping with the letter costs Mike nothing and would likely end Tommy's harassment out of gratitude.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is manufactured necessity: a request engineered so that any response, including a refusal, becomes contact. De Becker explains that the pursuer pushes buttons until one provokes a reaction and keeps pushing it as long as it works; guilt, harassment, and insult each work for a while and then fail, so the pursuer invents new hooks like the reference letter to keep the interaction alive.

assets.topic: The Button-Pushing Sequence: Guilt, Harassment, Insult
assets.visual_frame_description: A voice-mail inbox rendered as a timeline. Message bubbles scroll by in order: a guilt-trip message, a harassment message promising twenty bogus bookings, an insult message calling Mike an asshole, a written-apology demand, a 2 A.M. call threatening a formal complaint. Each bubble carries a label the player must match to its tactic.
assets.player_mission: Arrange Tommy's messages along the escalation sequence de Becker describes. Identify which tactic comes first, which comes next, and what the book says follows when victims participate.
key_concepts: The pursuer's real message is 'I will not allow you to ignore me.'
He will push buttons until one provokes a reaction, and as long as it works, he will keep pushing it.
Guilt is usually first, then harassment, then insult; each works for a while, and then doesn't.
When victims participate in this process, threats are not far behind.
Tommy moved from 'I've put my heart and soul into this thing' to 'I'm going to book twenty bogus trips with your agency every month.'
The insult campaign ('you are an asshole,' 'everybody wants to get away from you') followed the guilt and harassment stages.
A demand for a written apology shifted power by making Mike's compliance the precondition for stopping.
Mike's urge to respond after each new tactic is exactly what the pursuer is engineering for.
When Mike and Jackie stopped responding, Tommy's tactics could no longer land because impact is one of the few things a victim can control.
The victim and pursuer both come to share one trait: neither wants to let go.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the tactic-sequencing pattern: guilt first, then harassment, then insult, with threats not far behind when the victim participates. The book claims each tactic is a button the pursuer pushes until it stops provoking a reaction, so responding retrains the pursuer to escalate and literally buys another six weeks of pursuit.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Sequence and escalation of tactics across messages
assets.question: Tommy's campaign moved through guilt, harassment, and insult. Which reading of the sequence matches de Becker's model of how these pursuers operate?
assets.correct_cue: De Becker's model is explicit: "Guilt is usually first, then harassment, then insult. Each works for a while, and then doesn't." The sequence in the case maps onto it perfectly: guilt ('I've put my heart and soul into this thing... maybe you don't have the kind of commitment it takes'), then harassment ('You'll learn not to make promises you never intended to keep,' the twenty bogus trips threat), then insult and the written-apology demand ('I demand an apology, a written apology. You are on notice'). The critical cue is that the sequence only advances when the victim reacts, and the rule that follows is: 'When victims participate in this process, threats are not far behind.' Probing the threats themselves for intent matters less than registering that the sequence is being allowed to run.
distractors: The sequence is unpredictable improvisation, so no order or logic can be extracted from Tommy's messages.
Insults come first as the primary tactic, with guilt appearing only later after the insults fail.
Each new tactic means Tommy is cooling down, since anger fades as he vents it message by message.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests operant persistence: the pursuer's tactics are maintained by the responses they provoke. De Becker notes that the fascinating collapse at this stage is that pursuer and victim start to have something in common, neither wants to let go, so the victim's compulsive need to make it stop becomes part of the mechanism that keeps the war running.

assets.topic: Vague Language Feed: Maybe, Like, and the Fuel of Hedge Words
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen playback of the Fedder kitchen. On the left, Mike's de-escalation phrases appear word by word: 'might be leaving... in the next few months,' 're-visit the matter,' 'I'll let you know.' On the right, Tommy's face lights up after each phrase, translating each hedge into a commitment. A subtitle reads: 'Maybe = definitely.'
assets.player_mission: Scrub the hedged phrases in Mike's refusals for their role in feeding Tommy's attachment. Identify the mechanism Jackie names and select the phrase that most dangerously feeds a pursuer's belief.
key_concepts: Jackie observed that 'maybe' is sometimes perceived as 'definitely,' and 'like' can be taken as 'love.'
People who don't hear you don't hear you; at some point continuing to explain makes matters worse.
Talking encourages attachment when you are seeking detachment.
Tommy read a life-long partnership into a single seminar conversation and a business 'chat.'
Mike's 'if that happens, I'll call you' was heard by Tommy as an agreement with a timeline.
Tommy told Marlene that 'Mike and I are trying to get to the next inning,' rebuilding contact around a commitment Mike never made.
Mike's closing offers ('If I hear of any interesting openings, I'll let you know') gave Tommy another reason to keep written contact alive.
Every time the victim calls back after messages, it teaches the pursuer that the cost of getting a call-back is that many messages.
There is no straight talk for crooked people; logic cannot be taught to someone who doesn't speak the same language.
Contact is fuel for the fire, and for some pursuers very little fuel is needed.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the vague-language intake mechanism: hedged, softening phrases meant to avoid hurting a pursuer are decoded by him as commitments. Jackie Fedder's insight, that 'maybe' is perceived as 'definitely' and 'like' taken as 'love,' is the book's core claim here, because contact phrased kindly still encourages attachment when detachment is the goal.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Hedged language used during attempted refusals
assets.question: Mike tries to let Tommy down gently. Which of Mike's hedged phrases is the most dangerous fuel for Tommy's attachment, per the book's analysis?
assets.correct_cue: The deadliest phrase is the deferred promise: 'if that happens, I'll call you and we can re-visit the matter.' Tommy instantly rebuilt it as an arrangement, later phoning Marlene to learn her time frame because 'Mike and I are trying to get to the next inning,' and still later complaining, 'We had an agreement, you know.' The book's mechanism is Jackie's rule: 'maybe' is perceived as 'definitely' by someone who needs it to be, and people who don't hear you don't hear you. Any hedge that keeps a future open, especially one tied to a person or date, gives a pursuer a calendar to attach himself to. Final phrases like 'good luck in the world' also feed attachment, but the deferred-slot promise is what Tommy converted into an agreement with a timeline.
distractors: Small talk at the end of the call, like 'say hi to Jackie,' has no effect because it carries no business meaning.
A vague pleasantry such as 'I hope our paths cross sometime' is entirely neutral and cannot be decoded as a promise.
Explicitly saying 'we can just agree to go our separate ways' is wasted on Tommy only if it is phrased as a question rather than a statement.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is motivated interpretation: the pursuer processes ambiguous language through his desired outcome, so hedges become confirmations. De Becker generalizes this to romantic pursuers and ex-partners who don't let go: the victim keeps trying to communicate nuance, but explains that continuing to talk makes matters worse because it encourages attachment when the victim is seeking detachment.

assets.topic: JACA Risk Read on a Persistent Pursuer
assets.visual_frame_description: A threat-assessment dashboard splits into four quadrants labeled Justification, Alternatives, Consequences, and Ability. A case file for Drew, a 29-year-old who keeps texting after his breakup with Nina, streams quotes into each quadrant, some colored red, some green. The player must classify which quadrant is flashing an escalation warning.
assets.player_mission: Run the four general elements of violence (JACA) on a persistent romantic pursuer's messages. Identify which element signals elevated risk and which elements show he still has low-risk alternatives in play.
key_concepts: The four general elements of violence are perceived justification, perceived alternatives, perceived consequences, and perceived ability (JACA).
People likely to use violence perceive few or no alternatives.
Tommy scored low on risk because his continuing calls proved he saw many alternatives to violence.
Tommy showed no indication he was willing to give up his freedom, an intolerable consequence to him, by escalating to violence.
Threatening carried clearly tolerable consequences for Tommy, since even police visits did not deter him.
A pursuer who believes he must defend himself against an 'emotionally-involved assassin' perceives justification for lethal force.
Between the current conduct and violence there are usually several detectable warning signs.
Predicting without preparing is only curiosity; a management plan must follow a risk read.
Victims should evaluate the likelihood of violence and monitor new communications under management plan two.
If there is any reason to believe a pursuer might escalate beyond phone calls, intervention and contact with authorities should occur immediately.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the JACA framework, de Becker's four elements for judging whether a persistent pursuer is likely to turn violent: justification, alternatives, consequences, and ability. The book's claim is that violence risk rises as perceived alternatives shrink and as consequences become tolerable, while a pursuer who sees many alternatives, as Tommy did, is likely to continue harassment but not to escalate to violence.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Perceived alternatives, consequences, and ability in pursuer communications
assets.question: Drew, rejected by Nina, now texts: 'You're the only person who gets me. I've lost my job, my friends took her side, I have nothing left and nowhere to go. If you block me, I have no reason to hold back.' Which JACA element should alarm you most?
assets.correct_cue: The alarming cue is the collapse of perceived alternatives: Drew states directly that he has no job, no allies, and 'nowhere to go,' and frames Nina's block as leaving him with 'no reason to hold back.' In the Taylor case, de Becker notes that people likely to use violence perceive few or no alternatives, whereas Tommy's many continuing tactics (harassing, threatening, interfering with business) proved he saw alternatives and therefore scored low. The contrast is the diagnostic: a pursuer who still enumerates options is engaging in a campaign, while one who declares himself out of options and ties his restraint to the victim's cooperation is reciting justification ('I have no reason to hold back') with shrinking alternatives. The accompanying 'if you block me' condition is an intimidation framing, and the book's JACA lens instructs treating the declared absence of alternatives, not anger volume, as the risk signal.
distractors: The most alarming element is his anger volume, because loudrage reliably predicts imminent violence.
His many concrete complaints prove he is rationalizing, which is the same low-risk pattern as Tommy's harassment messaging.
Declaring 'I have nothing left' actually lowers risk because despairing people lack the energy to act.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests the violence-readiness appraisal: violence is chosen among perceived options, and each of the four JACA elements is a perception held by the actor, not an objective fact. De Becker contrasts Tommy, who saw harassment as one alternative among many, with Taylor, whose letters show justification, few alternatives, favorable consequences, and the purchased weapon, the ability component literally present.

assets.topic: The Apology Pretext in a Voice-Mail Audit
assets.visual_frame_description: A voice-mail inbox from de Becker's office, message waveforms stacked vertically with timestamps. The selected waveform plays Tommy's voice: 'I was just calling to apologize.' A transcript panel scrolls alongside, and the player audits whether the apology is genuine contact closure or a fresh engagement move.
assets.player_mission: Audit Tommy's 'apology' call to decide what it really is. Weigh it against his established baseline and the follow-up content in the same exchange, then render the correct diagnosis.
key_concepts: Tommy framed a call as an apology while simultaneously pitching the partnership again: 'I still think we can hit a home run with this thing someday.'
Apologies from persistent pursuers often recycle the original agenda, proving contact, not contrition, is the goal.
Mike told himself the matter was over because Tommy had apologized, and the pursuit resumed within a week.
Contact is fuel for the fire, and Tommy did not need much fuel.
Victims predict pursuer behavior by applying their own standards, which is exactly how a 'sincere apology' got misread.
With each contact, the victim buys another six weeks of pursuit.
The pursuer pushes guilt, then harassment, then insult, each until it stops working.
An apology that arrives with conditions or offers is a controlled transaction, not a peace offering.
The victim's stated plan ('I'll call him back and lay it on the line') had already been tried and had failed.
Jackie's rule governed the case: people who don't hear you don't hear you, so talking nine more times than you wanted is still talking to them.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the closure-stage deception: a pursuer's apology that functions as another contact device. De Becker's case shows the apology was immediately fused with the original pitch, and the pursuit resumed within days, illustrating that responses, even conciliatory ones, engage the pursuer and buy another six weeks.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Is Tommy's 'I was just calling to apologize' message a genuine apology that closes the conflict?
assets.subject_baseline: Across every prior exchange, Tommy converted Mike's statements into unspoken agreements: he phoned Marlene for a wedding-date timeline, complained that 'we lost two valuable weeks,' and described the ten-minute meeting as a 'business discussion we started.' Whenever the relationship was declared over, he answered with a new reason for contact rather than acknowledgment.
observed_nonverbal_log: 00:00:12 Call opens with 'I was just calling to apologize because I didn't want to burn my bridges behind me,' delivered in a bright, rehearsed tone.
00:00:31 Speaker pivots, no pause for acknowledgment, directly to 'I still think we can hit a home run with this thing someday.'
00:00:47 'I've put a lot more time into it, refining things. It's really come a long way' recited as if pitching, with rising energy.
00:01:02 No mention of the harassment, the insults, or the threatened bogus bookings; the apology covers only Mike calling Tommy's friend.
00:01:15 Call ends with 'I sure hope you haven't hired anybody to replace Marlene,' reopening the one condition that had been the original agenda.
interrogation_transcript: Tommy: "I was just calling to apologize because I didn't want to burn my bridges behind me."
Tommy: "I still think we can hit a home run with this thing someday."
Tommy: "I'm very committed to making this idea work and I've put a lot more time into it, refining things. It's really come a long way."
Tommy: "I sure hope you haven't hired anybody to replace Marlene."
assets.correct_diagnosis: The apology is a contact device, not contrition. It apologizes for one narrow item while re-opening every element of the original agenda within thirty seconds, and within a week the pursuit resumed via the 'reasonable request' of the reference letter. The message's function is to restart contact, which the book calls fuel for the fire.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The apology selects a trivial offense (calling the friend) rather than the harassment campaign, which is the tactic of minimizing wrongdoing to get a foot in the door. It is immediately followed by the original pitch ('hit a home run,' 'refining things'), showing the apology is a prelude, not an endpoint. It ends by re-injecting the single variable that had kept the fantasy alive (Marlene's position), which only makes sense if the caller still intends to pursue the partnership. Finally, Mike's belief that 'he has apologized and it's over' is the same error he made throughout: predicting Tommy by his own standards for behavior, the very assumption the book names as the most dangerous myth of intervention. Conclusion: contact-seeking disguised as closure.
distractors: Genuine remorse: the caller voluntarily narrowed his apology to the one offense that truly bothered him, prudently avoiding excuses.
Fear of consequences: the apology is a calculated attempt to head off the restraining order Mike's situation was moving toward.
Social politeness: having been raised to smooth over relationships, the caller is closing the loop as any courteous person would.

assets.topic: The Manufactured Emergency in Persistence Campaigns
assets.visual_frame_description: A smartphone notification screen fills the frame. Message timestamps stack upward: 1 message, then 2, then 5, then one flagged URGENT at 2:04 A.M., then 'formal complaint,' then the twenty-bogus-trips threat. Each notification is labeled with its claimed purpose while an audit panel asks what the real purpose is.
assets.player_mission: Audit the urgency and complaint claims in Tommy's message campaign to expose their manufactured function. Compare the claimed purpose of each message with its observed purpose, then render the diagnosis.
key_concepts: 'Urgent' claims from a near-stranger are a pretext for contact, since nothing about their shared business is urgent.
Tommy left a message at two A.M., an indication of escalating intrusion not governed by ordinary social rules.
A 'formal complaint' was announced without content, functioning as a new threat lever rather than a real legal step.
The twenty-bogus-trips threat ('You won't know what's me and what isn't') targeted Mike's business precisely because it would force Mike to respond.
Requests that appear reasonable exist to cement attachment or gain new reasons for contact.
Guilt, then harassment, then insult, with threats not far behind when victims participate.
The pursuer's message is always 'I will not allow you to ignore me.'
Police contact can encourage the very behavior it is meant to deter when it gives the pursuer a new engagement.
Keeping and evaluating each message turns the campaign into data for a management plan instead of fuel for fear.
Impact is one of the few things a victim can control.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the manufactured-emergency tactic: urgency claims and grievance announcements whose real purpose is to force a response. The book documents that after two weeks of silence Tommy's 'urgent' call, his formal-complaint notice, and his threat to book bogus trips all escalated on the promise of provoking Mike, confirming that contact, not information, is the currency of the campaign.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Tommy declares an emergency. Is the 'urgent' message a genuine emergency, and what does the surrounding pattern reveal about its purpose?
assets.subject_baseline: Tommy's baseline is contact escalation with invented destinations: promised ten-minute meetings that became forty, a 'business discussion' that had never been scheduled, an 'agreement' that was a chat, and a reference letter that was a hook. Each new contact retroactively re-frames the past as an arrangement, and each declares the next contact necessary.
observed_nonverbal_log: Day 1, 09:14: Call 1 and call 2 unanswered; message marks itself 'urgent' with no content.
Day 3, 02:04: Message left at two in the morning demanding an apology, adding 'You are on notice.'
Day 5: Message announces an unspecified 'formal complaint.'
Day 6: Message threatens 'twenty bogus trips with your agency every month,' claiming Mike made promises he never intended to keep.
Day 7: Message offers that an apology might be accepted, 'but we're getting to the point that an apology won't be good enough.'
interrogation_transcript: Tommy: "It's urgent I speak with you immediately."
Tommy: "Now you've ruined one of my best friendships, asshole! ... I demand an apology, a written apology. You are on notice."
Tommy: "I'm going to book twenty bogus trips with your agency every month. You won't know what's me and what isn't. Then you'll learn not to make promises you never intended to keep."
Tommy: "If you would call and apologize, I might accept that, but we're getting to the point that an apology won't be good enough."
assets.correct_diagnosis: The urgency is manufactured: each declaration is a lever designed to force the one thing the campaign needs, a response from Mike. The two A.M. call, the content-free 'formal complaint,' and the trip-booking threat share one function, raising the cost of ignoring Tommy until Mike engages, which the book identifies as pushing buttons until one provokes a reaction.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The urgency is empty by definition: no shared business, deadline, or hazard exists between a travel agent and a man he barely knows, and the message that follows apologizes for the friend-call, not for an actual emergency. The two A.M. timestamp marks an intrusion pattern that ordinary social norms do not permit, and chronology in de Becker's model is informative, not decorative. The 'formal complaint' appears without any named complaint, which is a harassment instrument, since its value to Tommy lies in its power to make Mike imagine consequences. The bogus-trips threat targets the business precisely because harming it would force Mike into action, a textbook effort to create consequences the victim cannot ignore. Diagnosis: an engagement weapon wrapped in the language of emergencies.
distractors: A genuine emergency: something in Tommy's personal life is about to collapse and he is reaching out to the only professional he trusts.
A legal escalation: the 'formal complaint' and the trip-booking threat mark the beginning of real litigation against Mike's agency.
A farewell ritual: these messages are Tommy's way of venting before he finally withdraws from the campaign.

assets.topic: Projection of Lethal Intent in the Taylor Letters
assets.visual_frame_description: De Becker's office desk holds Edward Taylor's typed letter to the district attorney's investigators. Annotations circle the phrases 'mindless, manipulative robopath,' 'paid or emotionally-involved assassin,' and '.38 handgun in his 46th year.' A mugshot-style profile of Taylor sits beside an unopened box labeled 'evidence: .38.'
assets.player_mission: Audit Taylor's letter to the D.A.'s investigators for what it reveals about the author. Decide whether the letter describes Hicklin or describes Taylor, and render the diagnosis the book reaches.
key_concepts: In the face of one's victim, one sees oneself (James Baldwin), the principle de Becker applies to Taylor's letter.
What Taylor projected onto Hicklin, that he was 'an emotionally-involved assassin,' was actually at work inside him.
Taylor accused Hicklin through a third party of 'paid or emotionally-involved' assassination after Hicklin had only sent investigators and letters.
None of Taylor's writings made a direct threat to harm Hicklin, yet the hazard was gleanable from the letter by applying the JACA elements.
Taylor felt he had justification to use violence: defending himself.
Taylor felt established authority did not care, leaving him few alternatives.
The consequences of violence had become favorable for Taylor because violence would stop the 'mindless robopath.'
Taylor had the ability to deliver violence: he had bought the gun.
The day he wrote about the .38, Taylor went out and bought one.
Interventions by private detectives, D.A. investigators, and police each escalated Taylor's grievance and his sense of threat.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests projection as a lethality signal: the subject describes his own lethal orientation as the attacker's trait. De Becker reads Taylor's 'emotionally-involved assassin' line as self-description and supports it with the JACA elements, each of which had been satisfied in Taylor's own mind by the time he wrote the letter.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Edward Taylor's letter complains that his life is threatened by a 'mindless, manipulative robopath' employing 'a paid or emotionally-involved assassin.' Who does the letter actually describe?
assets.subject_baseline: Taylor began as a flattering, fawning letter-writer ('Dear James,' 'You are a star,' a suggestion that Hicklin run for governor). Each invasive intervention shifted the baseline: after the private detectives' visit, his penmanship became erratic and the friendliness vanished ('You have grievously offended me'); he then adopted litigation as the focus of his life, then introduced threat-and-safety themes to the FAA, and finally grew preoccupied with weaponry and assassination imagery.
observed_nonverbal_log: Month 1, after the detective visit: Six-page letter, erratic penmanship, heavy corrections, 'You have grievously offended me... or is it that you are just simply Insufferably Arrogant?'
Month 3, to the FAA: Questions Hicklin's soundness of body and mind, calling him 'a threat to life, property and himself.'
Month 5: Demands an apology via civil complaint; calls Hicklin's presumed conduct 'emasculation at the door to one's own home.'
Month 8: Writes that a teenager might act out the 'sick fantasy as broadcast by Personality Pilot-Reporter-Folk-Hero Hicklin,' and condemns 'murder-by-the-torch.'
Month 9: Accuses Hicklin of a helicopter 'strafing mission' aimed at 'defenseless humans on the ground.'
Day of the final letter: Writes of a '.38' and 'paid or emotionally-involved assassin,' then goes out and purchases a .38 handgun.
interrogation_transcript: Taylor: "When a complainant perceives that established authority does not care and/or will not empathize with what it is like when one has his life threatened by a mindless, manipulative robopath..."
Taylor: "...to experience the trauma of purchasing a .38 handgun in his 46th year in order to defend himself from a paid or emotionally-involved assassin..."
Taylor: "Worst of all, is to consider the nature of complainant's alleged provocation against respondent (to hear the latter tell it): mail(!)"
Hicklin's staff, to de Becker: "We'll take care of it."
assets.correct_diagnosis: The letter is self-description: the assassin fantasy belongs to Taylor, not Hicklin. It states the justification ('defending himself'), the narrowed alternatives (authority does not care), the favorable consequences (stopping a 'mindless robopath'), and the ability (the gun he had already bought), and de Becker concludes that 'what Taylor projected onto Hicklin... was actually at work inside him,' with Baldwin's line as the interpretive key. Hicklin later died of a gunshot from the man he had never met.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The letter's own grammar reveals the projection: it is Taylor who carries the handgun, sees it on his desk at work, and faces it 'first thing in the morning,' while Hicklin's conduct consists of letters and an unannounced detective visit that produced no physical contact. The repeated words 'threatened,' 'trauma,' and 'defend' construct the writer as a besieged victim, which in de Becker's JACA framework supplies perceived justification. The line about authority that 'does not care and/or will not empathize' supplies the few-alternatives element, and the purchase of the .38 on the day of the letter is the ability element made literal. Because none of this was ever a direct threat, it was not prosecutable, but it was a hazard; de Becker's point is that the projection itself, not explicit threats, was the detectable signal of lethal intent.
distractors: The letter is accurate reporting: Hicklin did send private detectives, so Taylor's fear of paid intimidation is factually grounded and proportionate.
The letter is a cry for help: Taylor is describing his isolation and trauma to get professional mental-health support from the authorities.
The letter is a legal maneuver only: Taylor used dramatic language because he knew courts respond to emotional petitions.

assets.topic: Sinister Language Shift in Grievance Letters
assets.visual_frame_description: A document forensics timeline shows Taylor's letters morphing across the months: an ornate 'Dear James' in looping copperplate, then cramped agitated scrawl, then a typed complaint with words circled in red: 'strafing mission,' 'skeletal remains,' 'murder-by-the-torch,' 'offensive weaponry.' A header reads: 'Hazard assessment in the language itself.'
assets.player_mission: Audit the letter series for the language shift that separates a vexing letter-writer from a hazard. Isolate the moment the themes changed and render the correct diagnosis of what the language indicates.
key_concepts: Taylor's early letters were appropriate for the context: praise, remembrances, compliments, and a suggestion that Hicklin run for governor.
The first letter after the detectives' visit was six pages, with erratic penmanship and the friendliness gone.
The litigation theme became the principal focus of Taylor's life for a year after the detective intervention.
Taylor introduced the concepts of threat and safety when he wrote to the FAA questioning Hicklin's competency to hold a pilot's license.
His references turned sinister: 'strafing mission,' 'skeletal remains,' 'condone murder-by-the-torch.'
He came to regard Hicklin's helicopter as a weapon in the hands of 'mentally unbalanced men.'
At the start the situation was not interpersonal; after intimidating men warned Taylor to stop writing, it became interpersonal.
Jim Hicklin got the last thing he wanted: a relationship with Edward Taylor; they had become enemies.
The issue is knowing the differences between communications that portend escalation and those from which you can predict retreat.
Interventions that put a cost on Taylor's letters changed the letters' content before they changed his conduct.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests escalation-in-language: the movement of grievance communications from benign themes to threat-and-safety imagery is itself the warning sign. The book shows each intervention produced a qualitative shift in Taylor's letters, until sinister references and weaponry absorbed his writing entirely.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Across two years, Taylor's letters move from 'You are a star' to 'strafing mission' and 'murder-by-the-torch.' What does this language shift indicate about the situation?
assets.subject_baseline: Before any intervention, Taylor was a known tireless letter-writer whose letters amused or annoyed prominent Angelenos and were mostly ignored. His baseline was fixed, frequent, and non-escalating: same format, same praise, no development of grievance. The variable that changed everything was the first unannounced visit by private detectives with the order to stop writing.
observed_nonverbal_log: Baseline: 'Dear James... Respectfully Yours, Ed Taylor.'
Baseline: 'You are a star.' and a suggestion that Hicklin run for governor.
After the detective visit: 'You have grievously offended me... your presumed paranoia... or your naiveté... or is it that you are just simply Insufferably Arrogant?'
After the detective visit: Six-page letters, erratic penmanship, messy corrections, and the litigation theme that became his life's focus.
After the D.A. investigators: 'Does established authority not care... a mindless, manipulative robopath... the trauma of purchasing a .38 handgun.'
Final phase: 'Is there a more barbaric, mindless, obscene act than a pilot who would aim an aircraft at defenseless humans...'
interrogation_transcript: Taylor (early): "You are a star."
Taylor (later, to the station manager): "It is harassment; it is a virulent invasion of one's privacy; it is threatening; it is intimidating & it is Wrong!"
Taylor (to the FAA): "Until it has been established by your jurisdiction that Mr. Hicklin is of sound body & mind, I suggest he is a threat to life, property and himself."
Taylor (FAA complaint): "Is there a more barbaric, mindless, obscene act than a pilot who would aim an aircraft at defenseless humans on the ground for the sole purpose of harassment..."
assets.correct_diagnosis: The shift marks hazard formation: benign persistence has become escalating grievance language freighted with threat-and-safety themes. The content moved from admiration to offense to litigation to 'threat to life' to weapon imagery, exactly the progression that transforms a letter-writer into what de Becker calls a hazard, and it was driven by the interventions rather than by any act of Hicklin's.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The baseline letters contain none of the forensic markers, no threat, no safety language, no weapon imagery, which is why Carson's staff could safely ignore eight hundred similar letters from Searing. The first marker appears after the detective visit: offense language and erratic penmanship signal the intrusion was experienced as an attack, not a deterrent. The FAA letters introduce 'threat to life, property and himself,' transplanting danger onto the subject himself, which de Becker flags as the point where threat-and-safety themes enter the record. The 'strafing mission' and 'murder-by-the-torch' references are the final register shift, language of lethal imagery applied to an aircraft that in reality carried a traffic reporter. Conclusion: measurable escalation in fantasy severity, justification building, and the record shows the interventions were the accelerant.
distractors: The shift is evidence of deterioration only: Taylor's erratic handwriting signals a medical decline, not a behavioral hazard.
The shift shows the authorities' tactics worked: the letters grew angry because Taylor was finally being taken seriously and processed the lesson.
The shift is meaningless rhetorical flourish: angry letter-writers routinely exaggerate, and none of his words were actionable threats.

assets.topic: Benign Persistence Audit: The Searing File
assets.visual_frame_description: A Tonight Show corridor in 1980, a wall of filing cabinets labeled 'letters.' One drawer is pulled open: hundreds of identical envelopes. A man's photo, John Searing in a flannel shirt, is pinned above a chart tracking his letters over years, none of which change register. The audit question floats above: 'Is this persistence or hazard?'
assets.player_mission: Audit John Searing's eight-hundred-letter campaign against the escalation markers in the book. Decide whether this file is a hazard or benign persistence, and justify using the markers the chapter teaches.
key_concepts: Searing's letters, though they numbered more than eight hundred, never contained anything sinister or foreboding.
He maintained a job, had other interests, and above all never escalated the nature of his communications.
The Tonight Show made no effort to stop Searing from writing letters.
Carson's staff knew letters, no matter how frequent, can't hurt anyone, while starting a war can hurt everyone involved.
Had Searing been left alone, he would likely have kept writing for years, and that would have been fine.
De Becker's office has cases of people who wrote more than ten thousand letters to one media figure and never attempted an encounter.
The issue is not persistence but knowing the differences between communications that portend escalation and those from which you can predict retreat.
Searing never escalated the nature of his communications, the single most important differentiator.
Giving the pursuer exactly what he wants ended the campaign: Searing was told 'Now go and write no more,' and he did.
Media figures add fuel to the fire just by being in the media, yet Searing's exposure on the show did not create new pursuit.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the benign-persistence profile: high volume without escalation markers. The book's claim is that persistence alone is not sinister; the differentiator is whether the communications portend escalation (Searing's never did) versus those from which retreat can be predicted, and the Carson outcome confirms that failing to engage did not convert volume into violence.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: John Searing wrote more than eight hundred letters to The Tonight Show asking to yell 'Here's Johnny' on the air. Is this a hazard requiring intervention?
assets.subject_baseline: Searing was a thirty-six-year-old art-supply salesman from New Jersey with a steady job and other interests. His written requests began with a polite letter, continued through a refusal, a photo of Carson, and a form letter, and his response to rejection was simply to write again in the same format. Across the entire campaign the tone, subject, and escalation level of his communications never changed.
observed_nonverbal_log: 1980, Letter 1: Asks, since boyhood, to yell 'Here's Johnny' on the air; receives an eight-by-ten photo of Johnny Carson.
Letters 2-100: Repeats the request after receiving the photo, then after the form letter; starts enclosing audiotapes of impressions of Jimmy Stewart and Richard Nixon.
Years 2-7: Volume grows past eight hundred letters; no message ever contains anything sinister or foreboding.
Staff call: Asked 'why it was so important to him,' he answers flatly, 'Because nothing in life means more to me.'
Resolution: Flown to Los Angeles, seated at the desk, handed the script, and told 'Now go and write no more.' He went back to selling art supplies.
Follow-up: No further letters; the campaign ended when it was satisfied.
interrogation_transcript: Searing: "Because nothing in life means more to me."
Staffer (reading): "Thank you for your proposal... it would not be feasible."
Jimmy Stewart impression (on tape): "Let John Searing yell 'Here's Johnny.'"
Johnny Carson: "Now go and write no more."
assets.correct_diagnosis: Benign persistence, not hazard. The file satisfies the book's benign markers: no sinister content, steady employment, other interests, and, decisively, no escalation of the nature of the communications. The campaign was obsessive but structurally static, and its termination by fulfillment, not force, confirms that engagement of the right kind, or none, kept everyone safe.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The volume, more than eight hundred letters, is not itself a marker; de Becker's office counts clients with over ten thousand letters to a single figure who never attempted an encounter, so volume must be read alongside content. Every marker that would portend escalation is absent: no threat, no grievance, no safety language, no weapon imagery, no shift in theme mirroring Taylor's trajectory. The behavioral anchors (job, other interests) match the book's description of the letter-writer who can be safely ignored, and the variable that would turn volume into hazard, escalation of the nature of communications, never appears. Finally, the resolution, Carson giving him exactly what he wanted and Searing stopping, demonstrates that the campaign's currency was recognition, not harm. Diagnosis: static attachment with benign content; intervention would have been a war nobody needed to fight.
distractors: Hazard with escalation: the audiotapes prove Searing was trying to contact Carson personally, leaving letters for direct approaches.
Entitlement-driven hazard: the sheer refusal to accept 'not feasible' proves an unreasonable entitlement that routinely precedes violence.
Delusion: Searing genuinely believed he was in a relationship with the show, and delusion is the engine of all persistent-pursuer danger.

assets.topic: Engage and Enrage: The No-Contact Management Plan
assets.visual_frame_description: A night desk in de Becker's office. On the wall, two columns are labeled with chalk: 'Plan One: Change the pursuer' and 'Plan Two: Change how his conduct affects us.' Mike and Jackie sit beside a tape machine replaying Tommy's message as a new one lands with a soft beep. The player walks through the decision de Becker put to the Fedders.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the boss escalation by choosing the correct management plan for a persistent pursuer. In stage one, identify which plan the book endorses; in stage two, select the concrete no-contact response that stops the engagement loop.
key_concepts: The rule is called 'engage and enrage': the more attachment, whether favorable or unfavorable, the more the situation escalates.
With each contact, the victim buys another six weeks of pursuit.
You don't want the pursuer improved, you want him removed; efforts to change his mind or change him are the opposite of what you want.
As long as he gets a response, he is distracted from his life; each unanswered message tells him you can resist his pursuit.
The only way to have the desired outcome is to have no contact.
Mike had not even tried two weeks of silence, as Jackie pointed out.
Doing nothing provocative is itself a reasoned management plan and a communication to the pursuer every bit as clear as direct contact.
Under plan two, victims insulate from hazard or annoyance, evaluate the likelihood of violence, and monitor new communications.
What impact a harasser has is one of the few things a victim can control.
Time will take care of most people who refuse to let go; one drawer is for what you must act on, the other for what time will solve.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the engage-and-enrage rule: attachment of any valence escalates a pursuer, so the only management plan that works is changing how his conduct affects you, chiefly by not responding. The book's claim is that each contact buys another six weeks, and that appearing to do nothing is a reasoned plan that ends harassment faster than any confrontation.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Engage and enrage: every response the victim gives, whether favorable or unfavorable, feeds the pursuer's attachment and escalates the campaign, so the victim's lever of control is impact, not conduct. The book's evidence is the Fedder case: every escalation followed a contact, de Becker's estimate was six weeks of new pursuit per contact, and the campaign ended only once contact stopped entirely.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are replaying the Fedder file at the moment de Becker offers the two management plans: plan one, change the pursuer through warnings, counter-threats, and police interventions, all of which had already failed in this case; plan two, change the way the pursuer's conduct affects you by insulating, evaluating violence likelihood, and monitoring communications. Mike favors 'sending some people over' to explain the facts of life to Tommy.
assets.stage_1_question: Which management plan does the book endorse for Tommy, and which phrase from the case law of this chapter defeats Mike's counter-argument that Tommy 'has to' stop?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Plan two: stop trying to change the pursuer and change how his conduct affects you, because 'all terms were uncertain to Tommy,' he has no track record for logic, and 'there is no straight talk for crooked people.' Mike's plan-one instincts (a visit, a warning, police) had each already failed or backfired, exactly the pattern de Becker documents.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Two weeks of the no-contact plan pass, and Tommy's voice mail spikes: five messages in one day, a 2 A.M. call, and finally the threat 'I'm going to book twenty bogus trips with your agency every month. You won't know what's me and what isn't. Then you'll learn not to make promises you never intended to keep.' Mike's finger hovers over the call-back button.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Do not call back. Preserve the voice mail messages as evidence, route Tommy's calls to a new extension that my office checks hourly while forwarding everything except his messages, and continue monitoring for the detectable warning signs that would precede any escalation beyond phone calls. Calling back would engage, and engagement is the accelerant; instead, each unanswered message delivers Tommy the message that you can resist his pursuit.

assets.topic: The Intervention Myth: Watch and Wait vs. Sending the Detectives
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1971 Los Angeles den. A stack of pale blue letters sits on a writing desk, the top one reading 'You are a star.' In the background, two silhouetted men in fedoras walk toward a modest house, one door away from turning a letter-writer into an enemy. The frame splits into two timelines labeled 'Watch and Wait' and 'Engage,' diverging at the moment of choice.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the boss scenario by refusing the powerful urge to intervene. Stage one: read the early Taylor letters and decide the book's stance on sending private detectives; stage two: choose the correct response after the intervention has already gone wrong.
key_concepts: Believing that others will react as we would is the single most dangerous myth of intervention.
At the start, Taylor's letters were appropriate for the context; the situation was not interpersonal.
After the admirer was visited by intimidating men who warned him to stop writing, the situation became interpersonal: they had become enemies.
Jim Hicklin got the last thing he wanted: a relationship with Edward Taylor.
Letters, no matter how frequent, can't hurt anyone, while starting a war can hurt everyone involved.
Searing's case proved the alternative: The Tonight Show made no effort to stop him, and nothing bad happened.
Taylor's letters changed after each intervention: the detective visit produced offense and litigation themes; the authorities' visits produced threat-and-safety themes.
When there was finally a cost on his writing letters, the arrest for misdemeanor libel, Taylor stopped writing and stewed instead.
Violence is interactional: the reaction of a potential victim may distinguish a verbal altercation from a murder (John Monahan).
A strategy of watch and wait is usually the wisest first step; once engaging is applied, you cannot go back to watching and waiting.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the intervention myth: the assumption that others will react as we would, which drives well-meaning people to escalate situations that were safe. The book's evidence is the Hicklin case, where each escalating intervention converted a harmless letter-writer into a lethal enemy, contrasted with the Searing case where non-intervention produced no harm.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Watch and wait beats engage and enrage: the book's central caution of this chapter is that believing others will react as we would is the single most dangerous myth of intervention, and that engaging a pursuer converts a non-interpersonal situation into an interpersonal one and a war nobody needs. The contrast pair, Searing vs. Taylor, shows identical starting material, persistent fan mail, and opposite outcomes determined by intervention choice.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is late August 1971. A stack of letters from Edward Taylor sits on Jim Hicklin's desk: 'Dear James,' signed 'Respectfully Yours, Ed Taylor,' a suggestion that he run for governor, and one reading 'You are a star.' Hicklin's advisors offer to 'take care of it,' and a pair of private detectives stands ready to make an unannounced visit that will order Taylor to stop writing.
assets.stage_1_question: At this moment, before any confrontation, which action matches the book's teaching about the 'warning' the detectives intend to deliver?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Do not send the detectives. Taylor's letters are appropriate for the context and the situation is not interpersonal, and the book's rule is that letters, no matter how frequent, can't hurt anyone, while starting a war can hurt everyone involved. The Searing file rides alongside this moment: eight hundred letters left unanswered produced no harm, because the show never escalated. Believing a strong warning will stop Taylor is the dangerous myth of intervention, since Taylor does not react as we would.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The detectives went anyway. Taylor's letters have now turned: six pages of erratic penmanship, 'You have grievously offended me,' litigation themes, FAA complaints calling Hicklin 'a threat to life, property and himself,' and finally the accusation of a helicopter 'strafing mission' against 'defenseless humans on the ground.' Hicklin's people now propose the next rung: the district attorney's office, then arrest, each to 'make him stop.'
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Stop engaging at every rung: do not escalate to the D.A., do not pursue the libel arrest, and do not respond to the grievance. The book's evidence is that each intervention fed Taylor's grievance and his perceived justification (he later cited the arrest for three days in jail as the ultimate intrusion he could not recover from), and with no new cost or engagement his campaign would have no new fuel while being monitored for genuine escalation beyond letters. De Becker's rule governs the exit: a strategy of watch and wait is the wisest first step, and once engagement is applied it cannot be recalled; here the prudent move is to withdraw from the engagement ladder entirely, monitor, and let time take care of a letter-writer whose conduct, however obsessive, had still produced no encounter.
